utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Our next witness is Miodrag Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I say something? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. What was it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was in the witness room before I entered the courtroom, and I left my glasses behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Someone is already bringing your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- spectacles, and so far you've done extremely well without them, so let's hope that continues. You'll now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Miodrag Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 1st of October this year, did you make a statement to the Pavkovic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you read that statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I did read it before I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If you were asked all the same questions as in that statement today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is 4D504.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your statement you describe in detail your duties and your activities. Will you please tell the Chamber briefly about 1998, what was the post you held back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Back in 1998 I was commander of the 319th Signals Regiment of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Where was it based?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 319th Signals Regiment was at the Nis garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1998, did you as part of your work at any point stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Back in 1998, in my capacity as commander of the signals regiment and while I was training the members of the regiment, I was travelling around as commander for the purposes of this training and various drills. I spent some time in Kosovo and Metohija in March and in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: How long were those two visits?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: One or two days each. In addition to that, from July 1998 as units from the 319th Signals Regiment were actually active in the area, I in my capacity as commander would go to the area to see how the unit was doing and how they were going about their assignments. There were a total of three or four visits, and I stayed about one or two days each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. What about 1999, what were your duties in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999, in February 1999, I became chief of the communications organ, which was attached to the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you explain in detail about the scope of its work. Will you just tell the Chamber whether it was part of your duties in a purely technical sense to send reports to your superior command.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As chief of the communications organ of the 3rd Army command and based on a written request by the chief before the war broke out or the head of the communications administration, electronic communications and activities sector, I submitted daily reports in writing at the end of our daily activities. In these reports I provided information on the functioning of the communications system in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Again, in your statement you provided some technical and detailed explanations about all of this. Will you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what the situation was after the start of the NATO air-strikes in terms of the situation regarding the communications system in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw an analogy here about the communications system. I will tell you briefly how the communications system was set up to function in the time prior to the air-strikes. The organs and units, the communications organs and units of the 3rd Army, were fully operational and they were with the Pristina Corps. We also checked the communications systems and the command system. This check was conducted just before the start of the NATO air-strikes. The result was that this highly evolved communications system in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army, the focus being on the Pristina Corps, was providing no more than the bare minimum of conditions in terms of the command system. When the air-strikes began on the 24th of March, 1999, and when the Gora facility was targeted, which was the command post of the 3rd Army, when the Jastrebac facility was targeted, as well as the stationary communications centres, such as Kursumlija and Prokuplje, and regrettably these operations left 11 officers dead, one of them was a professional communications officer at Kursumlija and one was a professional soldier from Prokuplje. The communications system that was operating at the Gora facility was disrupted. This meant that the line of communication between the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina and the command post of the 3rd Army at the command building in Nis was disrupted. From this very first day and on each of the following days, specifically on the 25th, the NATO air-strikes continued on the stationary communications node at Mokra Gora as well as on the Prizren, Djakovica, Pec, Kosovska Mitrovica stationary communications centres and relay and wire communications and links were disrupted, which meant that it now became impossible for the Pristina Corps command and its subordinate units, that is, brigade commands, battalion commands, platoon commanders and the company commanders to submit information in the regular way. And it also became impossible for them to receive proper orders. This example that I mentioned, there were daily strikes by the aggressor on the facilities that were used for our stationary communications centres and stationary communication nodes as well as the external roads connecting these. As a result, the system gradually collapsed bit by bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You provide a very detailed account of all of this in your statement, Colonel. I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you. What about this situation that was ongoing during the war itself. Was this something that was reoccurring at various points in time? Were there any further disruptions; and if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Each strike on any of the stationary communications centres and nodes would cause a breakdown in our communications system. They would normally last 24, 48, 72, or more hours. Specifically I'm referring to disruptions to the following levels: Corps commands, brigade commands, battalion commands, and their links to company commands, as well as the links between company commands and platoon commanders. Again, I must go back to the situation that this brought about, as well as attempts that were made to enlist the assistance of forces belonging to the mobile communications system. They were securing some of the elements that were destroyed during these strikes against stationary communication facilities, and they helped to get the communications system up and running, back up and running, to some degree. So after this period, this was restored, but the capacity was greatly diminished. What I'm referring to is the number of channels that were available to all these command levels that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Any Defence counsel have any questions? You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis on behalf of the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have some questions for you based on your statement, which is Exhibit 4D504.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but can I please have a copy of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy for you here, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your statement was quite detailed, but I have to confess that some of the terminology was difficult for me to follow. So I'll ask you to explain a few things for me. In paragraph 20 you mentioned that from the 2nd of February you and some of the officers from the 3rd Army moved into the 3rd Army war command post in the Gora facility. And what is the Gora facility or what was it at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember what I said at the start of my evidence today. I made a reference to the Gora facility. This is a facility that in terms of engineering and how it was built and set up was meant to be protected from cruise missiles, from air-strikes, generally speaking, or attacks by artillery weapons. This Gora facility was prepared - and I'm saying this as a signals officer - to secure that the capacity of our communications system would be such that officers and COs and all the other staff of that particular command post could use it to its full capacity to maintain links with the subordinate units under the command of the 3rd Army. It made sure that they could have a line of communication with the staff of the -- command staff of the 3rd Army, and thus to ensure that there was a smooth command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in what town, what municipality was this located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This facility was in Toplicki Ustanak barracks in Kursumlija, Kursumlija municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I saw that in your statement, but I wasn't sure if that was all one location or we were talking about more than one. You mention in paragraph 27 a meeting of officers of the -- at the forward command post, I guess, on the 23rd of March, 1999. The 3rd Army commander, General Pavkovic, I take it, appointed a commanding group from among the officers, which included you and General Djakovic, Colonel Vranic and others. What was this commanding group that was appointed on the 23rd of March?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were all these officers and COs and civilians who were involved that I mentioned, and they were manning the forward command post of the 3rd Army. The army commander, General Pavkovic, had the following objective in mind. He wanted to use some of these officers that I mentioned to make sure that information could be obtained as quickly as possible, or rather, that orders could be issued to the subordinate units, those under the Pristina Corps command. It was for this reason that he was spending time at the Pristina Corps command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess I'm not clear, though, on what this commanding group is. Is this some sort of contingency in case the regular chain of command breaks down or certain individuals got hurt because of the war? What is this commanding group and how is it different from the normal positions everyone held?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is no different from any other officer group that were part of the -- part of the 3rd Army command at the forward command post of the 3rd Army. However, the army commander wanted to have an operative officer, a signals officer, an assistant for political work, an artillery officer, and whatever was required at hand. He would get people involved who were among the officers present at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 29 you mentioned a link to the 29th command. Can you tell me what the 29th command was. That's not something ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is what I'm talking about in this paragraph: The consequences of the NATO aggression as they related to the stationary communications system, and specifically the fact that the links were disrupted to a total of 29 different commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The way it's translated in English, it says: "In order to link the 29th command with all levels of deployment in the 3rd Army's zone of responsibility." It looks like that's referring to some specific unit or command, and from your answer I take it that's not correct, because I'd never heard of anything in the VJ called the 29th command and I just wanted to be sure I was right about that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you is that I have never before heard of what you term the 29th command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read the first sentence out for me in the original and we'll see how it gets translated here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: "This was about a large quantity of radio sets, radio relay sets, multiplex sets, with a total capacity of 616 channels that were no longer operational. These formed a total of 44 radio relay axes, and the purpose they served was to link all of the 29 different commands at all levels around the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army." Is that sufficient for your purposes, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That sounds a little different than how it appears on my written translation. In paragraph 33, the second sentence in English is translated as: "The impossibility of monitoring the movements of units presented a problem, as a result of which a large part of the PTK-2 remained in the unit utilisation sectors." Can you tell us what PTK-2 is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is what I'm trying to say, these were field telephone cables or PTK-2, and this is the type of equipment that the signals units of the VJ were using. However, because the quantity was insufficient and because it wasn't possible to move it around quickly enough on account of the NATO air-strikes, no moves or potential manoeuvres could be covered and no communication could be maintained to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You answered my question. Now I understand what PTK-2 is. I need to back up one little bit to paragraph 28. I forgot to ask you a question I had. In that paragraph you mention: "The average time for eliminating disruptions was 497.4 hours or 20.7 days." In that context can you explain to me what you mean by a disruption. Is that when a communications link is broken for whatever reason, is that a disruption?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I provide certain figures in this paragraph. These figures are in relation to the functioning of the radio relay link --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think you're answering my question yet. Can you tell me what your definition of a "disruption" is and then I'll have another question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. A disruption means that a radio relay line of communication that is established with a certain unit, for example, a line between the Pristina Corps command post and one of the brigades or between a brigade command and a battalion command is no longer functioning. This means that a stationary node has sustained damage, and therefore the devices being used there can no longer perform to their full capacity or function at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you say: "The average time for eliminating such things was 497.4 hours or 20.7 days." I have a hard time grasping that since the war only lasted 79 days. Three disruptions and there would be almost no communications for the entire time-period. Can you clarify for us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Part of the facilities after the NATO aggression could not operate at all; these radio relay communications did not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But this certainly must have been a contingency that you all in the VJ planned for before the bombing started. You've certainly anticipated that communications systems were something that would be targeted by NATO, and you must have had contingency plans and alternative means of communication, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the commander of the Pristina Corps in 1997 and 1998 asked the command of the 3rd Army to have preparations carried out of the units from the mobile communications system that would establish mobile communications centres and that would be an alternative for the stationary centres or nodes of communication. Since the communications unit of the Pristina Corps, the 52nd Battalion of communications, according to its organizational structure, could not meet these needs, there was no possibility for it to carry it out on its own, with its own signals units. It is from that point of view that the army commander looked at the 319th Signals Regiment, and on the basis of this request he ordered that a mixed unit, a mixed signals unit come to the area of the forward command post with the intention of it providing some kind of a replacement, even to a minimal degree, for a stationary system of communications, the one that was disappearing, going down the drain, as the NATO aggression went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, we heard earlier in the case from General Andjelkovic from the Supreme Command Staff, who talked at some length about the communications problems; we also saw a number of exhibits from the daily evening briefings held at the Supreme Command Staff, in which he or someone else from his section talked about attacks on communication facilities. It's clear that there were numerous problems and disruptions, but the overall picture seemed to be that communications were working, reports were going from the lowest level up to the highest, orders were being sent down from the highest to the lowest. Wouldn't you agree that in spite of all these difficulties and the bombings, that you did manage to maintain a working communications system throughout the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as for communications with the Supreme Command Staff, the existing communications system did provide for reports to be submitted to the Supreme Command Staff, or rather, to have orders received from the Supreme Command Staff. In this way it satisfied those needs. The focus of my analysis was the realisation of communications from the corps command to brigade commands, from brigade commands to battalion commands, and from battalion commands towards the commands of companies, and from company commands to squad leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, the farther you go down in the communications net, isn't it true, generally speaking, that the distances between the communicators grows smaller, shorter, they're closer to one another, and that alternative means, such as couriers, hand-held radios, other small radios can be used for those kinds of communication and don't necessarily rely on the stationary communication nodes you were talking about before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we talk about zones of defence that the brigades had, they were about 100 kilometres, or in some cases about 60 kilometres. Communications devices, I'm talking about small radios, that according to establishment brigades had as part of their equipment as well as battalions, companies, squads, did not make that possible in terms of their technological structure. When we're talking about couriers, that type of communications, where the communications organ or the chief of communications has the task of planning it and it is being carried out by couriers from appropriate commands, this is, indeed, carried through but at a huge risk because of the incessant activity of Siptar terrorist forces. I can give you an example. Signalsmen from the 52nd Mixed Artillery Brigade, when a wired communications line was being laid, were killed mercilessly, and a few of them were wounded by the Siptar terrorist forces in the period that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to show you a document that maybe you can help us with because of your particular expertise, and this is Exhibit P1052. We're going to try and put it up on the computer screen for you. There are three pages, and we'll go through them one by one. Can you see that? And you'll have to help me out because I only have it in Serbian and I don't speak or understand much Serbian. "Plan rada stanice veze," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I could kindly ask you if this could be enlarged, zoomed in. Now I can see. Thank you. In front of me -- Mr. President, may I -- may I speak once again? Before me on the screen I see the DV-6 form which represents a form, a communications document, as prescribed in the Army of Yugoslavia. It is called the work-plan of the communications station. In the right-hand corner there is a designation of the level of confidentiality. It says "military secret." This document is not filled out, and we do not see what the level of confidentiality or secrecy is. That was not filled out. In the line below what is entered is the type of route. In this particular case it is the radio telephone network. There is a section where it says "number." What is entered there is the number of the route. In this particular case it's the number of this network, which is 01. Further on it says: "For the period from" and the obligation there was to enter the exact date, month, year, and then it says "up to" or "until," and that should contain the same type of information. As for the next part, in this form what we see is the number where the successive numbers are placed in the mentioned radio network. Over here where it says "participants," "ucesnici," this was filled out in an inappropriate way because according to the rules on communication and the instructions on communications, there was the duty of entering the secret names of these five participants. Further on is the rubric that denotes the number for identification. That is established in a particular way, which is defined in special instructions. In this particular plan that we see here, that was not done. Further on there is a distinction between day-time figures and night-time figures. This pertains to information that has to do either with day-time or night-time. It has to do with atmospheric conditions affecting radio communications. Further on, frequencies, transmission frequencies and reception frequencies. Radio information is entered, or rather, relay information is entered for devices that have such capacities. In this particular case it says "K," which is probably for channel, 40, or rather, "R," which is reserve, equals 30. In the rubric that says: "Call-signs," "pozivni znaci," there is telegraph for the plan that is used for radio and teleprinter devices. There are numbers and there are letters that are used as call-signs. As for TLF, that means telephones, there are the following names: "Pastrik, Ibar-40, Osa-1, Osa-1, Kosa-1," and in night-time information, the information provided is identical to the ones that I explained as day-time information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of specific questions. The order in which the names are listed, is there any significance to that in terms of this communication net?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not understand the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Is there any significance to being number 1 on the list?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As for number 1 -- may I just have a look, with your permission, at the rest of the work-plan of this station. Can I please see the lower part as well. It says here: "Type of radio/network," and what is entered here is something. It says "Veza," "communication," he probably meant a linked radio network. That is what he should have written down here. So somebody is number 1, participant number 1, and that is the main station, namely, that this person calls the other participants and gives them approval to establish communications among themselves, if need be. However, since I've now seen this part of the work-plan, it was not filled out either in accordance with the regulations governing communications. We do not see where the station is placed, the type of work, the type of antenna, the power of the antenna, the frequency, the azimuth of the antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I understand that. I think you're getting beyond my question, though. You wanted to look at the bottom to see if that might help you answer my question about: Is there any significance to the fact that the number one party identified on the list is the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, precisely as I observed this second part of the work-plan, I could conclude that it is not official, it is not authentic, and it does not have a stamp, which is compulsory for the verification of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, that's not my question. This document is in evidence. My question was: Is there any significance to the fact that the number one party listed is the Supreme Command? Typically on this kind of form if you were filling it out, wouldn't you put the highest-echelon entity at the top, if you were doing it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't need to see this document to answer my question. If you were filling out this form for a communications net, wouldn't you put the highest-echelon entity at the top, whether that was the Supreme Command Staff, the 3rd Army command, the Pristina Corps command, whoever it was in that link, that was the one that would go at the top, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the task defined, as set by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Aleksic -- sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just thought that we should allow the witness to explain this document to the end. If I understood him correctly, he was saying that it did not have a stamp and that it was not filled out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, this document that is before you, was it filled out according to military doctrine? Have you ever written this kind of document? Would it have been done properly had you written it? And what is Pastrik anyway?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document that is before me is one that I certainly would not have filled out in this way, or rather, it would have to be filled out in accordance with the instructions on communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. There are four questions asked by Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Hold on. I can't hear two people at once. Right, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I read the transcript, there are four questions asked by Mr. Fila. Could we have them one at a time for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems a reasonable request, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way we're going to do it, Mr. President. One question is: Can he tell us whatever he can about this document; and then the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate question at this stage in the examination. If you have a particular issue that you want to put to the witness, then please do that, but a general question of that nature is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honour, it's just for the sake of time. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us, if you had filled out this document, would you have filled it out this way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not have filled it out this way because it is not filled out in accordance with instructions on communications documents. And as I've already said, there would have to be a stamp on it of the unit that, or rather, the command that had filled out this communications document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The document that you see in front of you, could -- would that enable the establishment of proper communication, as stated in the regulations for communication, if this kind of a paper were to be received?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking about the deficiencies involved, I wished to say that this document could not enable, ensure proper communications with these five participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, in your view, is this a document at all then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said in the beginning that this paper that is in front of me is a form that is used in communications documents, but as for being a document that creates conditions for ensuring proper, secure communications, that it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, my last question. You see here it says "Pastrik." As a signalsman, do you know what this could mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you please have this zoomed in. These are call-signs, call-signs. In accordance with the communications instructions, call-signs are established in a prescribed way through additional documents. Pastrik I hear for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question that I forgot a few moments ago. When you described the document as you see it here, you said that there is this number, 01, and then it said from the period from/until, and that is not filled out. Can you establish -- say the century in which this document was written?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President, that I chuckled, but since there is no such information contained, that is, to say the period from/to, all of this is guess-work, and I don't think it would be serious and proper for me to engage in that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Tomislav Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. Will you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Tomislav Mladenovic, son of Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, on the 27th of September this year did you not make a statement to the General Pavkovic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you read that statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were you to be asked the same questions today, would you provide all the same answers?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is 4D505. May it please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, please, briefly tell the Court about your military career, your duties, and the posts that you filled.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I filled a number of different command posts over a six-year period at a technical, operative, and strategic level. For 26 years I was involved in operations and staff work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Trial Chamber which post you were holding back in 1998.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 I was chief of the operations and training organ. This body was attached to the 3rd Army command. I continued in that post in 1999 until sometime around mid-February. As of the 1st of March, 1999, I was appointed to my new position as assistant commander for logistics in the 3rd Army. I remained in that post throughout 1999 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Will you please tell the Chamber whether throughout the summer of 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on. The statement you've produced said: "From 15 February to 1st March I worked as assistant commander for logistics." Now, should that be from 15th February for the rest of 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 15th of February, I had been in that previous post. Between the 15th of February and the 1st of March, I was involved in the handover regarding my new post as assistant commander for logistics. I was familiarising myself with my new duties, and there had been an order appointing me assistant commander for logistics and the date on that order was the 1st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, throughout the summer of 1998, did you spend any time at the forward command post of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. In 1998 I was part of the forward command post of the 3rd Army command. This began on the 27th of July and continued throughout the rest of 1998 until the end of the month of October, actually, which is when it was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that General Perisic, the Chief of Staff of the VJ at the time, throughout August 1998 was spending time in Kosovo and Metohija because he was touring units of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Chief of the General Staff, Perisic, with his team were touring the 3rd Army and its units in Kosovo and Metohija, and specifically in Pristina. I was a member of the forward command post and I was involved in the briefing as a member of the command of the 3rd Army. I was also involved in other activities, later on when an analysis was conducted, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 4D143 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document just by looking at the first page?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I most certainly do. It's dated the 14th of August, 1998, isn't it. The name of the document is: "Minutes from the previous analysis session following assessment and inspection of units in Kosovo and Metohija by a team of the General Staff of the VJ on the 14th of August, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we please switch to the last page of the B/C/S. In the English version this is the second-but-last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, please have a close look, items 3, 4, and 12 specifically. For the sake of precision, item 12 in the English happens to be on the last page.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 reads: "Create conditions for enlargement of the Pristina Corps and its engagement according to both peacetime establishment and, if needed, wartime establishment." If you would like me to comment, this is what I can say and this is what it means in practical terms. Conditions must be secured for the Pristina Corps under its peacetime establishment to get involved in certain missions, assignments; in other words, for it to grow, for manpower levels to be filled up to the level of its peacetime establishment because the rate was not 100 per cent. Also conditions were to be created and measures were to be taken should any orders to that effect be issued to switch to its wartime establishment, which means to have wartime manpower levels that were quite different from the peacetime ones and the scale was different because there were more men involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to move on to item 4? This is what it says: "Prevent DTS forces, sabotage and terrorist forces, from spilling over from one territory into another, crush them within the blockade sector." This is what's being ordered here. One is to foil any movement by the sabotage and terrorist forces from one sector to another. Also, while doing this, these forces are to be crushed in whichever sectors they happen to be in in order to forestall this spillover and to keep them from re-emerging and continuing their terrorist activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Okay. Item 12, please, General, if you can.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Item 12 reads: "Recruitment must be carried out at all levels in order to at least maintain current levels. The order of the NGS for recruitment to PRK units must be ready by the 20th of August, 1998, at the latest, in exact accordance to the VES based on requests by the army command." Yes. This item is related to the previous item, which I believe was item 4 or even 3; it's about the expansion, about the growth, of the Pristina Corps to the very maximum of its peacetime establishment. Because this was not the case, not in terms of soldiers, not in terms of officers, the Chief of the General Staff is hereby issuing an assignment to the -- those in charge of this in the General Staff and the command of the 3rd Army, to do whatever necessary to bring up the manpower levels in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 4D416.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet. Can we zoom in a little? Yes, I do. This was issued by the General Staff of the VJ, the date is the 17th of August, 1998. It bears the following title: "Measures to further strengthen combat-readiness." This is an order issued by the Chief of the General Staff following his tour of the units of the 3rd Army and the inspection in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Please briefly comment on items 3 and 4. In the English these are page 2; in the B/C/S item 3 is on page 1, item 4 on page 2. Please briefly comment on item 3 first, if you can.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in slightly. It's not particularly legible as it is. All right. It's fine now. Thank you. This item talks about the following: "Units of the 3rd Army, especially the Pristina Corps, with reinforcements must prepare as a priority to engage along and secure the state border." This is fine and this is how it should be shown in the future because now I can read. "Units of the 3rd Army, with the focus on the Pristina Corps, with reinforcements ought to be prepared as a priority to engage along and secure the state border," yes, yes, "facing the Republic of Albania and Macedonia in the border belt, if necessary even further afield, whereby they will be securing all along the border and down the depth of the territory the state border. The involvement of some of the forces should be planned to secure and defend all military facilities, commands, and units throughout Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, General.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I will tell you something about the essence of this because I have just read it back, haven't I? This is how we would have understood this at the army command and what sort of orders we would have issued to the Pristina Corps to deal with this. There is one thing I wish to point out. The task of defending the state border, it's not as in the previous case, just about securing the state border, which is something that is done by the border units, because they're not actually defending, that's not what they do. The order here is in relation to the border belt, which was extended to 5 kilometres, and that is where this defence of the state border was to be carried out. But there's this particular bit of wording added even further afield. What this calls for is the involvement of additional forces from the Pristina Corps in keeping with the assessment along the axes where the dangers -- where the danger came to forestall any movement, any entry by sabotage and terrorist groups from Albania and Macedonia into Yugoslav territory, and vice versa, to prevent these groups from going to Albania to get their weapons there, and such-like. Further, facilities are to be defended behind the army lines as well as manpower and equipment. This is normally something that guard security does and guard security had already been stepped-up for a considerable period of time. But the order here is to defend. What does that mean? That means that units belonging to the Pristina Corps must be used across this area, because if you defend a certain facility, a barracks, for example, or a building, the Pristina Corps command, any storage facilities, military depots, that sort of thing, this is not something that you can do effectively from inside, from the building or facility itself. Then you're certain to meet a bad end. You have to do this from outside to really defend these facilities, to make sure that you do. So that's the meaning of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can we now go to page 2 of the B/C/S, item 4, comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In this item, the spillover of sabotage and terrorist forces from Kosovo and Metohija must be prevented into the Rasko-Polimska territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Slow down, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: "As well as the Jablanica and south Morava areas -- sectors. Continue coordination and concerted action, joint action, with forces of the MUP and in keeping with assessments, provide support to the MUP forces in their effort to crush sabotage and terrorist forces to a degree that will not significantly affect the implementation of the fundamental tasks of the VJ units."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, be so kind and tell the Trial Chamber, what is the Rasko-Polimska sector. Where is the Jablanica sector? Where is the south Morava sector in the Republic of Serbia. Explain the location of all these places.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The order here is to foil any spillover from Kosovo and Metohija into the Rasko-Polimska sector. This is north-west of Kosovo and Metohija. It's not part of Kosovo and Metohija. If I had a map, I could show you. Likewise, this spillover should be prevented. The Siptar terrorist forces must be stopped from actually crossing into that area. That's what spillover means. It's a term much used in the military. Spillover into the Jablanica sector or south Morava sector. That's what it says at least. We don't know specifically what they mean. So this is to the south, speaking from a purely administrative point of view, in relation to the area covered by Kosovo and Metohija. So what is this about in purely practical terms? One must prevent any movement by the sabotage terrorist forces, first and foremost to the south, facing the Republic of Albania and the Republic of Macedonia, as defined by the previous item that we looked at. And on top of that, both the east and the west must be secured in relation to Kosovo and Metohija, the area east of Kosovo and Metohija and west of Kosovo and Metohija. This order does not say that forces should start action only along the area north of Kosovo and Metohija, which in administrative terms borders on central Serbia. In order for this to be implemented, as envisaged by this document, this effort would have required a significant involvement on the part of the Pristina Corps for this assignment to be completed. The army command must certainly understood well what this order by the Chief of the General Staff meant and implied. They produced an order for the army command. It was probably a more detailed order, but I can't remember right now, on how to operationalise these assignments. I am certain that the order faithfully reflected these assignments. They may have been presented in a more specific form and also in a more operational form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have Exhibit 4D418.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't managed to comment on the latter portion of the item. I'm not sure if you want me to or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, my mistake. I'm really sorry. Will you, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Because it is much broader than that, isn't it. So the latter part of this item says that: "Support should be lent to the MUP forces in their effort to crush the sabotage and terrorist groups to such a degree that would not significantly affect the implementation of their fundamental tasks." This position that support should be lent to the MUP forces is self-explanatory. The only thing I have to add is about the degree that is specified, such a degree that will not significantly affect the implementation of the fundamental tasks. Based on what I said before, the fundamental tasks of the units of the 3rd Army, and the Pristina Corps above all, was to secure the state border. There is now this order by the Chief of the General Staff. It says: "To defend," defend, "the state border." Now, this was the case in all previous orders. Furthermore, the next vital task is to defend military facilities, materiel, and manpower, defend manpower and secure facilities would be the exact wording, but that is something that we have in our rules, and one must make sure that the life and work of the Pristina Corps could unfold smoothly, which involves the Pristina garrison, and in particular the units along the state border. Their vital interest would be at risk if this assignment was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may be a good time for a break because I'm about to move on to my next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, we have to have a break at this stage; that will be for 20 minutes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, I just wanted to apologise for my disruption. Apparently, my personal communications were working too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's bound to happen occasionally, Mr. Hannis. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please call up in e-court 4D418.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was better a few moments ago. Maybe it should have stayed the way it was, but I'll do my best. Yes, I can see it now. This is a document of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the sector for operations and staff affairs, the 24th of August, 1998. I see that it is in the form of a telegram. The document was sent to the commander personally or the Chief of Staff, to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comments regarding paragraph 3 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see paragraph 3, could you scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. This paragraph regulates, I'm reading it out: "In keeping with the needs and possibilities, support the MUP forces in crushing and destroying sabotage terrorist forces, bearing in mind that the level of combat-readiness not be impeded of commands and units in carrying out their basic tasks." The content of this paragraph actually relies on the previous order of the Chief of General Staff that I spoke of; however, what is highlighted here is the support of the forces of the Ministry of the Interior. Of course what is borne in mind are the basic tasks that the army, or rather, the Pristina Corps had in the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we are going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 4D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is a typographic map on which a decision is depicted of the commander for crushing the sabotage terrorist forces in the area of the village of Ratis. The map shows a graphic representation of the action that was planned to be carried out in this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what is written in the upper left-hand corner of this document, this map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is customary -- or not customary, this is the way it's regulated in the rules on combat documents, that the commander should give his approval. Here it is specifically the approval -- it says: "I approve," and then the name and surname of the -- that is to say, the commander's decision is approved by the commander Lieutenant, or rather, Colonel-General Dusan Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Because I brought many documents to the commander to sign, I know what his signature is. As far as I can see, it is the commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please call up on e-court 4D504. Your Honours, because time is short, we did not manage to have the entire document translated, but the part that we do have translated is an official translation by CLSS. So we're looking at the heading and we're looking at a particular paragraph that I'd like to hear the witness's comments on, but we have the entire text in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the rest of it to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honours. Just a moment. Your Honour, I do apologise for this pause. The right number would be 4D508, so could we please have that document called up on e-court. Could the B/C/S version please be displayed on the other page, the page -- the second page, paragraph 5, and in English we just have this one page so could we keep that. And I would like to look at 5.1 in the Serbian version. Yet another page to go in the B/C/S version. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please be so kind as to have a look at this and could you look at the second paragraph, the following words: "I have decided ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why have we lost the English? Sorry. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read the second paragraph within paragraph 5, the one that says: "I have decided..." et cetera. General, this is just a partial translation that is there. Could you please make an effort and read it even though it's this way so that the Trial Chamber could see the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. It says here: "Continue to intensify (combat groups of the army) to support MUP forces in surrounding and routing the DTS in the general sector of Kramovik. Engage some of the forces in preparations to block the villages of Donji Ratis and Gornji Ratis." I see down here the signature of the commander of the 3rd Army. I didn't see the beginning, it's probably a combat report, where paragraph 5 was part of the content of this report. This is certainly the way reports are done. Because of course, as authorised by the commander, I signed this document and submitted it to the superior command, or rather, the operations staff of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. So that is the document involved. And what is done here is an order is issued for the further engagement of forces. I want to say for all of paragraph 5 that it is an integral part of combat reports and it means that the commander of the subordinate unit - in this case the commander of the army - sends to the superior command - in this case the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia - their decision on the engagement of army forces, specifically this mostly has to do with the forces of the Pristina Corps but then there were the other army forces there as well, for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up in e-court 4D496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that means that this document is a combat report being addressed to the General Staff by the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So could we please have 4D496 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document, or rather, this map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We were a bit faster.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document. It is entitled as: "A survey of the deployment of forces at the end of the fourth stage," that is the disposition of forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, it has to do with the forces of the 3rd Army, notably the Pristina Corps. And this disposition of forces, as represented graphically on this map, was approved by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think I have the right map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're going to move on to the next document that has to do with this particular topic until we resolve our problems here. Could we please call up in e-court 4D451.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, this is the English version. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It would be right if this could be zoomed in, the command of the 3rd Army -- yes, now I can see it, yes. It's a document of the command of the 3rd Army, dated the 18th of October, 1998. This is a regular combat report which was submitted to the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia from the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see paragraph 5, subparagraph 2; in B/C/S it is page 2 and in English, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can you give us your comments on paragraph 5.2?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. 5.2 is entitled: "Situation," meaning the situation in army units, and what is reported here is that combat groups from the Pristina Corps took over sections. It is stated here which combat group took over what section. It also includes the actual figures pertaining to every one of the units in combat groups and what the equipment they have is. This was, generally speaking, the content of combat reports. Daily information was provided in this way, depending on what was relevant and important for that particular day. This was an obligation in terms of carrying out a specific order, in this case of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and a deadline would usually be provided, but if a deadline was not specifically stated then it -- it meant that a report would be included in the regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. After the agreement was signed with the Kosovo Verification Mission, or rather, with the OSCE, what post did you have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the organ for operations and training and staff affairs, however, with a special -- by a special order by the army commander, after the forward command post of the command of the 3rd Army was abolished on the 30th of October, 1998, that is the date when it was abolished, by an order of the commander - I don't know when exactly it was issued, perhaps a bit before that day - I was appointed head of the team for liaising with the organization for security and cooperation in Europe in Kosovo and Metohija. It was called KVM in its English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 3D785.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is a document that was drafted by the liaison team of the command of the 3rd Army, liaising with the OSCE, that is; specifically this has to do with a regular, weekly, report for the period from the 18th until the 24th of December. The document was sent and registered on the 24th of December, 1998. You will probably see the signature there. You will see that I signed this document, this report, as head of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just one question before that. Throughout your tour of duty, did you send such reports from the liaison team to the General Staff, you or your deputies, that is?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By the order of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and in keeping with the order of the command of the 3rd Army, it was regulated that daily reports should be provided by the liaison team to the command of the 3rd Army and weekly reports on the realisation of tasks. This submission of weekly reports was directly and specifically derived from the agreement where it says in a particular paragraph that state organs of the Republic of Serbia shall submit to the mission weekly reports on movements, situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say, of their own forces. So daily reports were written, whereas these were summary reports. They certainly contained the activities that were reported on in daily reports. It's the same structure that was used for these reports, but it was in one place, and it was the duty of the liaison team of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to submit this report to the appropriate organs of the OSCE team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake, we need the first page of this document, paragraph 1 on the first page, and then paragraph 3 further down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And if you can read that and give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph reads that: "On the 21st of December, 1998, between 8.00 and 2.00 in the afternoon, a movement was carried out of a military column consisting of 23 combat vehicles; three 30/2, two-barrelled 30-millimetre, tanks, mortars there; 120 mm BRDM, armoured reconnaissance vehicles, three; and one TZI, recovery vehicle, along the following axis: Batlava - Bajcina trig point 716 (the Jablan feature) and vice versa." This paragraph and all the other paragraphs that pertain to the forces of the 3rd Army moving about in Kosovo and Metohija is something that the liaison team of the General Staff of the VJ got regular reports on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 says that: "At 0800 hours on the 19th of December a reinforced 15th Armoured Brigade, tank company, consisting of 20 combat vehicles, 15 non-combat motor vehicles, and 165 soldiers and officers, went to the Batlava airfield sector to carry out planned exercises pursuant to the unit Combat Training Plan and Programme." Should I comment on this? I would be happy to. The Pristina Corps was reinforced indirectly with soldiers that were trained already. It wasn't the case that individual training was done anywhere in Kosovo and Metohija or in the Pristina Corps. It was said that no untrained soldiers should be sent to the area because the area was dangerous. They would receive individual training across the units and behind the lines in central Serbia. Once a soldier arrived at the Pristina Corps there would be individual training, but that was all that was done. It certainly was desirable for every soldier to be trained to perform tasks required as part of the establishment from the lowest possible level, squad level, up to the tactical levels or company and even battalion, so that to all practical intents this particular activity, the training itself, in a particular area, this was done by the 15th Brigade of the Pristina Corps. As far as I'm familiar with the agreement with the OSCE, the activity was not limited to that, and I'm pretty certain that I'm quite familiar with it. The corps command was responsible for training their own troops, especially bearing in mind its surroundings and the situation that it had been facing for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the outset of your evidence you said that on the 1st of March, 1999, you became assistant commander for logistics at the 3rd Army command. Can you tell us this: Was the medical service, too, part of the logistics organ?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The organization of the logistics organ of the 3rd Army command comprised the medical service. This was one of the seven services that were part of the organ, and not going into all the rest of them, but the answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit 4D354 brought up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I can see it. This is a document produced by the command of the 3rd Army dated the 20th of April, 1999. The heading is: "Battle-field clearance, supplement to order."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 1, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: "Send Captain First Class Milos Kostov, a pathologist from Nis military hospital to join the PrK team for battle-field clearance on the 21st of April, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that this particular pathologist, Kostov, was there on a particular mission or was he simply sent out as a permanent reinforcement? Did he remain there until the end of all combat operations? Do you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This document was produced at the command post itself. It was authorised by the commander and was first forwarded to the military hospital so that it could carry out this particular assignment. It was also forwarded to the logistics organ at the rear command post. I was assistant commander for logistics, and the medical service under me, and we were in charge of monitoring the activities of the Nis military hospital, and we were to see to it that this order was carried out. Captain Kostov was dispatched in keeping with this order, and the duration of his stay was not limited. He was to carry out his tasks as soon as he reported to the Pristina Corps command, until further notice, that's what it says. This is a supplement to an already-existing order on battle-field clearance, as it reads, and the request is probably for him to join the teams already involved in clearing the battle-field or perhaps one of the investigation teams, but there should be more specific order by whichever commander was in charge at ground level. But I know that he was dispatched there and he was to remain until further notice and for as long as his presence was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyone else have questions? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me just one minute to organize myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. I am Branko Lukic; I represent General Sreten Lukic. I only have a couple of questions and I want to pick your brain. I want to use your experience and see if you can help us explain a couple of things. This will not be a cross-examination true and proper as we know it. You do have a copy of your statement in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No, in fact I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to talk about paragraphs 21 and 22 of your statement. The kindness of our technicians is helping me along in this and we'll soon have these paragraphs on our screens, this is page 4 in the B/C/S that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on paragraphs 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, if perhaps you find that easier, do you want a hard copy in front of you? I could provide one.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If you need your own copy, I'll do my best to follow it on -- to follow on the monitor in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine then.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Should I address the issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you read paragraph 21, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph you talk about Defence Exhibit 4D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please bring this exhibit up in e-court. Could we please have 4D495 brought up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree that what we can see on this map, a decision by the commander to crush the sabotage and terrorist forces in the Ratis sector, is a representation of the respective positions of the VJ forces as well as the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this decision in actual fact a component of an order?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This decision, this map, is a visualisation of a combat order. It visualises, it represents, what is envisaged in the actual combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll down slightly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, there is something there that is circled in red towards the bottom of the map, the 52nd Combat Group?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Combat group number 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Indeed. I think it's actually the 52nd Military Police Battalion, maybe it's not clear in your copy.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is the 52nd Military Police Battalion just above, but the last thing I see down towards the bottom is the combat group -- 52nd combat group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're quite right there. My mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 6D698 brought up in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what this is about. What sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a combat document, an order, produced by the Pristina Corps command. On the last page you can see who actually issued the order, and we can have a look if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an order to support the MUP forces in crushing the sabotage and terrorist forces in the general area of Ratis village, right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us first bring something up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please, both in the English and the B/C/S. We need 5.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 5.3, General, reads: "The 52nd Military Police Battalion shall attack along this axis: Suka Vogelj-Porobica-Donji Ratis village with the following task: In cooperation with a part of the forces of the 8th MUP Detachment and the Djakovica PJP company ..." Is that consistent with what we saw in that decision on the map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The axis of operations of the military police that was marked there is probably reflected in this document. These should be compared. The axes -- their respective axes should be compared with the ones that we see on the map, and then we can base our conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another question about this document, sir. Something about item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 6 in the B/C/S and page 7 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a part of an order to do with command and communication. There is a mention there of coded maps, maps in code. We are mere laymen here. Could you please be so kind as to explain in layman's terms what that means. Why are these important and what is their purpose, why they're made.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. Maps in code are produced for tactical units, companies, and so on. Certain locations are defined in code and reports are based on this. Whoever is listening to this reporting process has no idea what they're talking about. That is the simplest possible explanation. This is normal at lower tactical levels normally using encrypted communications secure lines, but these are smaller units so a map in code was quite acceptable. A commander would use this to base his reports to his superior commander on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that axes of operations are marked on these maps for any assignments?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
