utterances.text: It depends. If it is an attack, if it concerns an attack, then this is represented in graphic terms, where a particular unit acts. That is the way it is done. That is how maps are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Every commander sees his role on this map and also the tasks of his unit and those of his neighbours. Is that customary?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The axis of his engagement. I didn't give you a full answer. It is customary when an order is given to a particular unit, then it says in narrower terms, This is the task, and then through a manoeuvre or in concert with another unit get to such and such a line. This is practically a representation of what was written in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We just want to have a complete transcript. Thank you. As you've already said, these maps are handed over to commanders of units that participate in the action concerned. Can we, therefore, conclude that maps were given to commanders of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia as well as the commanders of the units of the MUP that are marked on these maps that are decisions?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said, not me. The commander of the unit concerned makes the map, his superior commander approves, it is his map and it reflects his decision. The superior commander approves the map. The superior commander does not draw the decision of the subordinate commander on a map and then hand it over to him. However, as for a map that was done by a higher level and that pertains to several units, he sees his place and his role, and then that part that he is supposed to carry through, he elaborates. He makes a combat document, an order, he represents it graphically on a map. The commander hears his idea as to how the decision should be carried through, and if it is in line with the order of the superior commander, then he approves it. He says, I accept your decision, please go ahead, and then he works out the combat order as a combat document, and the content of that order is graphically represented on a map. Once this is done, then he brings this map to his superior commander for him to see, and then he approves it with placing his signature in the upper left-hand corner. That's the procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously I as a layman made a mistake, because in our vocabulary there is a difference between commander, in the sense of komandant and komandir in the sense of commander?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Up to battery level and then there are commanders in the sense of komandant at the higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Commanders of -- commanding officers and leaders of lower-ranking units that are marked on these maps, do they get the part of the map showing their unit and its axis of action? That's what I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that a company leader can get it. He doesn't work out these combat documents. He does not write an order. He does not work on a written document, and he does not draw a map. He gets his order from the superior commander orally. He makes an assessment. He conveys his decision. He is not duty-bound to draw a map or to write a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanations.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: He can get an excerpt, that's all right, but it's not obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to paragraph 22 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we move on, the questions are being asked of you to establish whether or not the commander of a MUP unit acting along with VJ would ever have issued to him the map or a part of a map that had been prepared for the operation. Now, you've indicated that orders are given down the chain orally, and while a map may be in somebody's hands, some inferior officer's hands, that is not obligatory. Are there any circumstances in which a MUP officer in charge of a MUP unit involved in such an operation would be given a diagram or map setting out the task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. I don't know how this is regulated in the Ministry of the Interior and with the MUP forces. What I was saying pertains to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you do understand. The question relates to the VJ map. Are there any circumstances in which the MUP would be in possession of a map prepared by a VJ commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I see no reason for that, because the army command made maps for their own units. And if the MUP units are of interest, then they're on the map. However, giving a MUP officer the map, I don't see that would be necessary, and after all it's not regulated that way either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you don't know how this is regulated in the MUP. Have you ever seen a map for carrying out combat activities made by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off except for the speaker's.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never in a position to see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please now move on to paragraph 22. You say: "I participated in creating the document 3D697. This document is an analysis from the 2nd of October, 1998, and was written by all the organs of the command of the 3rd Army at the IKM in Pristina." I'm just going to ask you about the methodology involved, how it is that we got certain figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For our purposes could we see on e-court page 9 in B/C/S and 10 in English. Could we zoom in on column 5, please, Ratis, since that is what we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This breakdown is attachment 3, attached to your document. In column 5 we see Ratis --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the fifth line you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we see from there the number of personnel involved in this action?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's portrayed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the final outcome of these columns, save for the Army of Yugoslavia, was obtained in the following way. All the personnel taking part in all actions were added up?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. All the individual numbers were added up of persons taking part in individual actions, and then this was sublimated. If we look at the numbers involved in each and every action we see what the grand total is, how many people were involved in all actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here it seems that in these nine actions, 56 combat groups took part. Is it correct that there weren't that many combat groups in Kosovo, but that it is this methodology that added up all people in all actions led to this number?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. You're quite right, certainly. Of course I know that there weren't that many. There's an exact order of the army commander and the General Staff, where groups were defined at this level. So it's 10 or 15 groups as far as the army is concerned. It was either 10 at one point in time, and then another five were established on the basis of a decision by the army command. I don't want to speculate now, but I think it was 15 or 16 groups, that's it. No -- oh, I wish there were this many.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This pertains to the number of personnel, right, so this count led to this number of people as well?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've dealt with that already, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We lawyers are sometimes boring and we have to ask questions that seem unnecessary to other people. The same pertains to the police as well, right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the charm of you legal people. Yes, of course, it pertains to the police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can also see the JSO here. It says that there were three units, and we all know that there was just this one unit, the JSO, if you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was just one; however, I do allow that the Ministry of the Interior knows better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. No further questions for you. Thank you for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Hannis for the Prosecutor. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could you tell us what rank you held when you retired.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I retired on the 1st of July, 2002, as lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, you told us that, I think, from 1st of March, 1999, you worked as assistant commander for logistics in the 3rd Army command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where physically were you located during that time, from the 1st of March through the end of the war, in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of the war I was at the logistics command post that was located in Nis. According to a certain plan, I also toured army units in the area of Kosovo. As far as I can remember, I was on tour twice and both tours lasted from one to two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you made those tours and where you went specifically in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when I went. There was some time in between, but I know exactly where I went. I toured the 202nd logistics base that had its command post in the village of Banjska. I also visited a part of the 202nd base, which was located in Klina. I was at the command post of the 3rd Army -- the forward command post, rather, of the 3rd Army that then coincided, rather, it was located at the command post of the Pristina Corps. That's where I met the army commander and the corps commander. That is basically where I was engaged. I did not go out to control the joint forces because from a professional point of view I was in charge of the logistics bases, and the logistic base was resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps; and that is why I went there to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that in 1998 you were part of the forward command post of the 3rd Army command, beginning on the 27th of July until the end of October 1998, when it was abolished. Where was that forward command post located?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The forward command post was taken -- was located in the barracks of Kosovski Junaci in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why was that forward command post abolished in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The forward command post of the command of the 3rd Army in 1998 at this location was abolished by an order of the superior command. However, if one were to ask what the reason was - now this is my opinion - it was due to the fact that the basic tasks that the army had until then had been carried through, and there was no need for it to remain there any further. And that is why it was abolished. A forward command post, and forward command posts in general, of subordinate units are established by the superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did its abolishment have anything to do with the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement and the creation of the OSCE and the KVM?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that exactly, because -- well, first of all, on the basis of this agreement forces were withdrawn that were outside the establishment of the Pristina Corps. Then forces from the area of the Pristina Corps were withdrawn into military complexes or barracks. So the composition of forces that were engaged in Kosovo and Metohija was far less extensive than before, and therefore it was probably not necessary to have a command post there any further. I am not ruling out the possibility of this agreement having affected the situation, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to look at Exhibit 4D416.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one you talked about earlier, General, it's the 17 August 1998 document about measures to further strengthen combat-readiness. And I think if we could go to -- do you recall looking at that before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page, I think it's item number 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second sentence in there it's translated in English as: "Continue coordination and joint action with MUP forces and in keeping with assessments, support the MUP forces in destroying the sabotage and terrorist groups ..." From that is it fair of me to conclude there must have been prior joint action and support of the forces of the MUP, since it says "continue." So I gather that was going on before this point in time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. If it says "continue," then that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on your position and being stationed at the forward command post in July to October 1998, you do know there was a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina at that time, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about any Joint Command or any body called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You never heard of it before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I had previously heard of the expression "Joint Command." I had heard this expression at the forward command post, but what this expression meant to me and everybody else at the forward command post -- well, I don't know about everybody else, do I, but I do know about myself. This to me meant activity by the Pristina Corps command with the MUP command staff in Kosovo and Metohija, and this was about coordinating actions. This was about having cooperation between the army and the MUP, maybe coordination at the level of cooperation where the Pristina Corps command was involved and the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, that was my information at least. But this was about cooperation. That was the level. The Pristina Corps command was not superior or subordinated to the MUP staff or, indeed, the other way around. So that's what it meant. Yes, the expression was bandied about, so when the Pristina Corps commander made a decision, it would be approved by the army commander to lend support to the MUP forces, and then the Pristina Corps commander would take an operative officer, go to the MUP staff, or they would go to the corps command, I'm not really sure how this worked because I wasn't there myself, and this is one thing that I do know and that is what the expression meant to me, Joint Command, but I'm not aware of any body actually existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there may be a translation problem, I'm not sure. I'm told that in 55, line 8, when he was first asked about it this, he said: I didn't know about any Joint Command or any organ that was called the Joint Command, I don't know if that's different, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was about a body, and I said I didn't know about any body. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I need to follow-up on that, I guess, because in English when I say "a body," it can mean either an individual human being or it can mean an organ, I guess, is the term that is translated for a group of people. Either way, were you aware of any human being or group of human beings that were known as the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija meeting in Pristina in 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Body organ command, body and organ, it's about body parts, right, but for something to be a command it needs a structure, an organizational structure, and this must be defined by appropriate documents. An organizational structure must have organs, and I believe that now we can use the word organs that are in charge of certain functions. At the head of that body there is, for example, a command, and then you have a commander. These are rules governing work in the VJ. I did not know of any such body. A command of sorts, well, I probably would have known about that and that command would have been part of a command system having to do with the army, the MUP, or a third party. I probably would have known, but I didn't and I do not, not the way you defined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me try it this way because we've had this problem with other witnesses. Now, whether you call this body the Joint Command or whether you say it's a coordinating body or whether you call it the Pristina branch of Hell's Angels, are you aware of a group of people, including General Pavkovic, General Lukic from the MUP, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, Mr. Matkovic who met in Pristina in the summer and early fall of 1998?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I never said "body" nor did I give the possibility to say that somebody was somebody's branch and so on and so forth. As for this structure you're telling me about now, what you're enumerating, I don't know. I'm not competent to talk about that. I was at the forward command post of the army command. What I said to you, I know that, I was there, I confirmed that. I know that the expression at the forward command post figured in that way. I do know that as far as coordination with MUP staff was concerned, General Pavkovic went there and Colonel Jankovic went there. They said, We're off there to coordinate this, to agree on this, with the MUP. Who else was there is not something that I know. What I don't know, I can't say, can I? I was there -- had I been there, had I seen this, I would say so or maybe it was, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you did know that General Pavkovic and Jankovic, was he a colonel or a general at that time? Let me ask you that first.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I said already that General Pavkovic went with Colonel Jankovic to this coordination meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't know who any of the other people were that went to these meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. I never needed to know. What mattered to me was that there was a representative of the army who was involved in a joint task with the MUP, and that had to be agreed there. Anything else was not my business. I had my other tasks, to which I devoted all my time. This was a command at an operative level, it had it own purview, this was within its purview pursuant to the rules governing the work of corps commands, they had to have coordination with commands of that level, from the MUP specifically, to exchange information, and it was on this task where we were supposed to lend support to the MUP, and that needed coordinating. They did that on their own. There was no need for anyone to mentor this process or supervise this process and that there was no such thing for lower command levels when they have something like that and when somebody to monitor or supervise them, no, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it from that and your earlier answer, that you personally never saw any documents purporting to come from the Joint Command or any VJ documents referring to the Joint Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw any documents with that type of heading or origin arrive at the forward command post of the army, but I can't rule out the possibility that there are certain documents that refer to the Joint Command. There are references to that in certain minutes that were taken at the forward command post, certain records at the forward command post. Those are documents that say that the commander of the Pristina Corps, after his decision was authorised, was going to the Joint Command to agree coordination with the MUP organs. I did see those references in documents, but a document from a Joint Command and me seeing such a document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you did see a document referring to the Joint Command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- probably. I can't rule that out. There may have been a reference somewhere that it was supposed to go somewhere to the Joint Command, the expression being used, but maybe not. If I saw a specific document, maybe I could tell you. There were all sorts of documents produced by various organs. I don't know if there was a reference to that or not. I don't know for sure. Somebody may have written things like these. The commander went to a coordinating session with the Joint Command, somebody may actually have used the expression. I can't rule out the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems to me, though, General, we've asked similar questions of some of the other military witnesses, that you as a professional soldier, if you had seen a document come across your desk making reference to a Joint Command, wouldn't that have aroused your curiosity, because command is a very specialised and important concept for professional soldiers. So wouldn't you want to know, What's this Joint Command? I never heard of it. I know the 3rd Army command, I know the General Staff, what's this Joint Command? Wouldn't that have made you curious and caused you to investigate if you had seen such a document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Investigate, no, that wasn't my job. That was other people's job, other organ's job. But I did have an idea about the expression Joint Command, and it was no surprise to me, but I never pictured a command, an actual command when I said that and there was nothing that really piqued my curiosity and there was no need for that on top of everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I can understand why you might have less curiosity if the document that came across your desk said "coordinating body," but Joint Command, as I say, seem to have a special military significance. But you say it wouldn't be your job to investigate something like that; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That was about what you said earlier on, about me investigating that, other than that a Joint Command is not a term that has any particular technical significance anywhere in the VJ. If you look at all the rules, you won't find a single reference to that type of command, nor indeed can it exist. Therefore, for me, the issue has no relevance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The oddity for -- speaking for myself, is that that's exactly the situation where you would expect a man used to dealing with the concept of command to be concerned. If the regulations rule out such a body, when you see a document emanating from such a body or referring officially to it, should it not ring bells and require you to check up what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the documents that I produced, that I was responsible for. I never used that expression myself in any of those documents. I never saw a document marked as the Joint Command. If another organ used that expression, well, I must say I wasn't really receiving many of those documents, not that kind. I wouldn't look into that because those documents were not my responsibility. I never used the expression myself. I consider it to be a mere expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have one other question in regard to this. When was it that General Pavkovic and Colonel Jankovic were attending these coordinating meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the work-plan of the forward command post, when the Pristina Corps on the next day was supposed to, for example, carry out a certain action and then the corps commander would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you misunderstand me. What time of year was this? First of all, which year was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This occurred in 1998. It was part of the orders that we looked at previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And bearing in mind the position you held then, what were the circumstances in which Pavkovic would tell you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavkovic had no need to tell me in person. He would say that and everybody from the forward command post was there. There were about ten officers there, including the army commander or the Chief of Staff. He would receive approval for the decision to lend support to the MUP forces and he would say, I'm off to the MUP or Jankovic would say something. This was an expression that was used, We're on our way there to agree on a decision, so this was some sort of a Joint Command, and this was in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell me who gave General Pavkovic approval for the decision to lend support to the MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Samardzic or the Chief of Staff, if he happened to be at the forward command post and the army commander was away, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we break now, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mladenovic, we have to have a break at this point; that will be for half an hour. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we bring up Exhibit 4D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, this is a map you looked at earlier. I think this is one involving a proposed operation in the area of Ratis village. Hopefully, it will be on your screen in a second. Maps take a little longer because they're such big files. Do you have it on your screen now, General?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can't tell, is there a proposed date for this operation on the map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Would there normally be on a map like this or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It should be marked according to the instruction on keeping combat documents, that is to say instructions for the work of commands and staffs. So the date should be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll to the bottom of the map. I want to be sure before I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't see anything at the bottom of the map. We've had some other maps where in the lower right-hand corner there would also be a name and a signature. Is that a standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It is standard procedure to have in the upper right-hand -- lower right-hand corner to have the author of the map, the name, and the rank, and also the signature of the appropriate commander of the relevant command, who is in subordination to the officer whose name is in the upper left-hand corner and that he got the map from. I don't see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what does the absence of that information on this map signify to you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That fact indicates to me that this job had not been completed, that staff work was not present to a sufficient degree. The staff officer taking care of this was duty-bound to take care of it. The name was supposed to be there and it was supposed to be signed. Maps are usually done by staff officers. Commanders, or rather, these officers take it to their commander so that they would see it, so it is really the fault of or omission on the part of the staff officer and the commander probably did not have the time to see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if this is important, Mr. Hannis, but I don't think I understand -- I'm just trying to move it. I don't think I understand who is supposed to sign where.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll follow-up, Your Honour, if I can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was my understanding from some of our earlier maps and earlier witnesses that in the upper left-hand corner was usually the name and signature of the superior officer or commander who was approving the proposed map, and the signature in the lower right-hand corner was by the subordinate officer who had created the map or was proposing the operation depicted on the map. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. As I said, this was -- well, what is important for this map is the substance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer what you're asked, because that leaves outstanding who the reference is to in the upper left-hand corner, line 24 of page 63, which is where I become confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mean the phrase about: "And that he got the map from"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that part confuses me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll deal with it if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, you've also referred in your answer to something being in the upper left-hand corner. What should that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the upper left-hand corner what is written is that the map is being approved and who it is that approves it, the rank, the name, the surname. And then the map is verified by a signature, and thereby considered to have been approved, the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, and in fact I've been unfair to you, Mr. Hannis, because I see you've actually asked the question that way according to line 15, but I heard "right-hand" I think, although it says "left-hand" in the -- so I've caused utter confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well I thought I was clear about that, that signature in the upper left-hand corner is the superior officer who approves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is all my mistake, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think. But my problem is there is reference to three people in the answer that was originally given. There was the lower right-hand and the upper right and the upper left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe the upper right was a mistake, I don't know. If you look at line 20 of page 63: "It's standard procedure to have in the upper right-hand" and then it changes to lower right-hand. So, maybe if that can be clarified we'll have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if you can be patient with me for another minute. Then, in the upper left we have the superior officer, the commander, who signs signifying his approval of the operation proposed on the map, correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, just as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: However, this is not an operation, this is an action. Operations are much bigger. They have to do with the use of corps as a whole. So these are combat actions. There is a difference involved. That is a far lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that. Can you tell me where the dividing line is between an operation and an action, how many units are involved before an action turns into an operation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In order to call something an operation, it has to be carried out at least at corps rank; that is to say, that this corps can have 15 or 17 brigades, and that is between 3500 and 5.000 people. That is to say, up to 10.000 people. Action is combat action, a combat activity, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would not have more than how many men, more than a thousand?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be more than 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now let me get back to the map. In the upper right-hand corner of this map, what information do we see there in the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Up there we see the degree of secrecy where it says "defence state secret," that is the highest level of secrecy or confidentiality. Also there are other levels, strictly confidential and confidential, respectively; however, this is the highest level: Defence state secret. It is decided upon by the officer in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's a standard procedure on all maps and that's where it always goes is in the upper right-hand corner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the lower right-hand corner is where you would normally expect to see the name and signature of the author of the map or the proposer of the action or the operation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the rank, or rather, where the post is, as in commander, and then the rank and then the name and surname. That is written by the draftsman, and then the commander has to sign it, the one who created the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the left-hand corner does any information typically go there or is that normally blank, the lower left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, there is a key there, and that is usually done when the composition involved is very complex. For small maps like this, it is quite clear, green is MUP, red is army units, and blue are the terrorist forces. There is no need to have a key for this because this -- these are standard markings. It would be superfluous here. It's not necessary to do it at all on maps like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you now explain to me whether the person who signs the bottom left signs first or -- the bottom right, rather, or whether the person who signs the top left signs it first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First the lower right, the commander who brought the map for approval and for the map to be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how can this map contain the approval, as it does, without having the name and signature of the person who sought approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible when the officer who goes with the commander did not finish this, the commander did not notice this, the superior commander does not check this, previously the map was not given to the professional organ of the command from where it is brought to double-check it and see if everything was done right, and then the officer who accompanies the commander, he submits it, the commander signs it, and that's the end of that. So certain omissions were made here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, then, while we're looking at this map, it proposes a joint action involving both MUP and VJ forces, correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a graphic representation of action by MUP and VJ forces. The proposal contains the engagement of army forces to support the MUP forces. The commander gives approval for the engagement of army forces, the superior commander, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to follow-up on a question I think that Judge Bonomy asked you when Mr. Lukic showed you another map, and that is: How, if you know, how would the commanders of the MUP forces - I don't know if these are detachments or what size they are - but of these MUP forces, how would they know where they were supposed to go and where their positions and axes of movement were vis-a-vis what the VJ forces were doing unless they had a copy of this map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: MUP forces that are depicted here in order to be able to carry out this task have to have the same map, because this content of the MUP here is based on decisions made by the staff of the MUP or the organ in charge in the MUP. I wouldn't like to define that, probably a MUP staff or some command, for the engagement of MUP forces. In relation to that, what was planned was support to the MUP by the army. According to this logic, the MUP would have to have an identical map, except that it would have to be approved by the competent authorities of the MUP in this way. After all, this is prescribed through their own rules and regulations, and I really would not be competent to interpret that. That would be logical. But really, I do not have any insight into that combat rules, the way they are used, and also how their combat documents are regulated. I simply do not have such information available, and this is not a subject I dealt with during my professional career. How the MUP professionally plans the use of its forces and what documents are a basis for the use of their forces. However, in order to carry this out correctly and in a coordinated manner, it has to be identical. However, there is an appropriate MUP command standing behind the use of the MUP, and as for the army it is depicted here who is behind that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Bear with me for a moment. Just getting down to the basic, simplest level, then somebody draws up this map initially. Would that be somebody in the VJ or somebody in the MUP, if you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If a military operations officer is preparing the map for the commander, then it is going to be drawn by an operations officer of the army; however, he has to know before that what forces are going to be engaged by the MUP and what kind of support he needs. When the MUP forces are depicted to him, how they're going to be engaged as well, and that he is asking for such and such support, then he depicts the deployment of the military; and that is the end of the job as far as the operations command of the army -- operations organ of the command of the Army of Yugoslavia is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a practical matter, how does a copy of this map get into the hands of the MUP? Does somebody in the VJ make an exact copy and deliver it to the MUP so it can be distributed to those commanders in the field who are going to need it? Physically, how does that get done?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I did not participate in that process, how the MUP submitted combat documents to their subordinates. I really don't know. I simply don't know. There was no need for me to know that or did I see that in the case of any MUP organ, that a copied map have been given to them with the signature of the commander of the army. There were some maps that were signed by General Pavkovic. Perhaps this had to do with speed. I assume that it had to do with speed rather than insufficient professionalism, although the two are related. However, this kind of map, for it to be used as a base for a MUP understanding -- MUP use, I don't understand this and I did not see the MUP using a map like this because I was not directly engaged with them. I was mostly engaged in tasks that were being carried out by army units and the focus on the border, et cetera, so I did not take part in this technical work to see how this was done in their situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, I don't know if there's an equivalent Serbian expression for something we say in English about the devil is in the details, meaning, for example, it may be easy to make a big plan, but working it out, the logistics and all the little things you have to do to accomplish it is what we refer to. Do you understand the concept I'm proposing when I say "the devil is in the details"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: We say "djavo" for devil, that's the word that's to be used. But if the latter is not there, then the operations level, the strategic level, cannot do a thing, the higher level. So yes, this is concretization. This is where, ultimately, tasks are being carried out, so it's got to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wouldn't you agree with me then, in the case of trying to effectively implement joint operations between the MUP and the VJ, it would be useful, if not necessary, to have some sort of body to coordinate that or, perhaps, command it, and that's the very kind of thing a Joint Command could do and did do in Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: If the security forces - because that's what they're called too, according to the law - the army and the MUP are referred to in that sense, if they were to be structured by having, that is to say the MUP and the army, to have units for carrying out such tasks, that would be excellent. However, this painstaking job of coordination was indispensable in order to have this carried out, or if somebody had authorised the army to command the MUP or authorised the MUP to command the army, it would be far simpler, whereas this way, this coordination on a footing of equality is what happened. I'm not going into whether -- to what extent it was successful, but it does require quite a bit of effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, could you have a look again at 4D416.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think you addressed him by the wrong name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I heard Radinovic, Your Honour, but I see it's correct on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope I said Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard Mladenovic. I heard Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's good enough for me, Mr. Mladenovic. 4D416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are a number of things in this document, and at one stage you told us that when you're referring to spillover from Kosovo being prevented, that the reference there was to the north-west of Kosovo and Metohija. And then you went on to say: "The Siptar terrorist forces must be stopped from actually crossing into that area. That's what spillover means. It's a term used in the military. Spillover into the Jablanica sector or south Morava sector. That's what it says at least. We don't know specifically what they mean. So this is to the south, speaking from a purely administrative point of view, in relation to the area covered by Kosovo ..." And then a little further on you say: "And on top of that, both the east and the west must be secured in relation to Kosovo. The area east of Kosovo and Metohija and the area west of Kosovo and Metohija." Now, I'm trying to understand these references to south, east, and west. I understand what you were saying about north-west, but west of Kosovo is Albania, is it not, and south of Kosovo is Albania and Macedonia? So what were you saying in that section of your evidence about the nature of the task being assigned to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: May I? I will explain it slowly. The Rasko-Polimska region is outside the area of Kosovo and Metohija geographically speaking to the north-west, in the Republic of Serbia, and it has an administrative line dividing it from the central part of Serbia. The Jablanica district is to the east of the area of Kosovo and Metohija, just like the southern Morava district, as is written here, but I think it's called the Pcinja district. To the south is Macedonia and Albania. Practically, from that task there, from the Chief of General Staff, what was ordered was to make sure that from the area of Kosovo and Metohija there is no spillover or not to allow a transfer of terrorist forces or for them to cross over to Albania, Macedonia, the eastern part, that is to southern Morava district, as stated in the order of the Chief of Staff, the Jablanica, and also Rasko-Polimska region, so it is only not towards the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now understand that clearly. And does that amount to deploying the VJ along - and I use this word in the broadest sense - along the border between Kosovo and Montenegro and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That means that the army has to prevent the spread of terrorism -- terrorist forces from here, but not Serbia but exactly regions as stated here, Rasko-Polimska, then the central part, towards the central part of the Republic of Serbia, Pcinja, Jablanica, Rasko-Polimska region, all of that is central Serbia. That is to say, to prevent a spillover of sabotage and terrorist forces from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija to the areas mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. I'll tell you why straight away. Yesterday we received notification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladenovic, you spoke about the fact that the 3rd Army at one point -- and I'll ask you about 1998. I don't want to know about anything else. You said in response to a question by the Chamber that it was sometime in the summer of 1998. All right. So that -- in the summer of 1998, that General Pavkovic went to that, to those meetings, to reach agreements with the MUP. The first question I wish to ask you is this, can you answer this one for us: How long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Until September, I think, when the actions were completed. If you look at when the last action was completed, so that is the time we're looking at. I don't think it went any further than October. I don't know for sure, but if you look at the last operations and the dates coincide, but it didn't spillover into October, or rather, it didn't exceed October.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Second question: The forward command post, you said when General Pavkovic came there, about actions that were to be taken the next day and sometimes General Samardzic was there and sometimes there was the Chief of Staff, and we know that was General Simic, don't we, do you know what time of day the general came, General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This was regulated by the work of the forward command post that subordinate commanders should be there at about 1800 hours or 1830, and that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Did General Pavkovic after that go to these meetings for those agreements or whatever we choose to call that with the MUP organs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after that, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there was a desire to change something, to amend an order received by General Pavkovic from General Samardzic or Simic, would General Pavkovic go back to see Simic about that, about the possible amendments or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if there was a need felt by the MUP for further support for more forces to support them in relation to what the army commander or the Chief of Staff had authorised at the forward command post, General Pavkovic would go back and then he would present this, he would say that they had additional requests, additional needs, and the army commander would approve that or not approve that, depending on what decision he took in each specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: General Simic was heard before this Trial Chamber, and he said this -- his decision was law to Pavkovic, and Pavkovic had to live by that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That is perfectly in keeping with the rules governing the functioning of the army. There is a popular saying: An order issued by a superior officer is law to his subordinate officer. This is a popular saying in the -- in command theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right let's not waste any more time. You explained about this command system, right. Yes, you have. In the last sentence that the Prosecutor asked you he said that it was their claim, and that maybe somebody else's claim, too, that the Joint Command, the body called the Joint Command, exercised command over units of both the army and the MUP in Kosovo, right. Throughout your time there in 1998 and everything else that you told us about, everything else you did there, have you ever come across a suggestion that somebody exercised command over both you and the MUP and that the name of this someone was the Joint Command? What do you think about this position, about this belief?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I've never heard this belief expressed, really, this position presented. As far as the army is concerned, I know that, I can say that, nobody else could possibly have exercised command over us outside the army itself. So if you have the Pristina Corps in addition to the army commander, who was there at the forward command post? Nobody else could possibly have exercised command over it and there would have been no need for anybody else to exercise command over it. If we leave that aside for a moment, Commander Pavkovic really cared very much about subordination. Whenever there was something that was ambiguous he would always go back to the army commander and he never allowed any interference in his own command structure. Even when I tried to bring up some things with my subordinates without his knowledge he would always be furious about this, Who is this Mladenovic, what has he got to say about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. That question was inappropriate, no one objected to it, but again you're going way beyond what is necessary when you're allowed the privilege of re-cross-examination, Mr. Fila. And you must appreciate that the type of answer that's just been given is one that might well led to a request by Mr. Hannis to ask more questions and you've all had your turn already. This is not the proper way to conduct this additional form of cross-examination. We allow you to avoid prejudice. This was not a question necessary to avoid prejudice. Now, if you have any more that need to be asked, please ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question: We spoke - and you referred several times in answer to many different questions - that there had to be some form of coordination between the MUP forces and the army forces on the ground. You said about the fact that back in 1998 the army was coordinating with the MUP, they were lending the MUP their support, and so on and so forth. My question: Is it necessary for a third party to do this or is it possible for the army itself to coordinate its actions with the MUP without anyone's intercession? How exactly did that happen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That would not have been necessary. If there had been a third party, they merely would have hampered the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, does anything arise from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, from the answer the witness gave, I did have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you said at page 77, line 5: "Commander Pavkovic really cared very much about subordination. Whenever there was something that was ambiguous, he would always go back to the army commander and he never allowed any interference in his own command structure ..." Sir, are you aware that General Pavkovic was noted on more than one occasion going over his direct commander, going directly to Mr. Milosevic; that is, he went over General Samardzic when Pavkovic was in the Pristina Corps and he went over General Ojdanic when Ojdanic was the head of the General Staff, do you know about any of those --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to that question because there's no evidence of that. There are -- there's that letter from Perisic that contends that, but there's not any evidence that he ever went over anybody's head in terms of the Joint Command. Just cause he has a meeting with Milosevic doesn't mean he was going over somebody's head in the Joint Command. This is an inappropriate question because he suggests to the witness there's evidence to support this. There are allegations that might support this, but no evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's not confined, of course, to the Joint Command, but to the circumstances that we've heard about in the course of the evidence. Mr. Hannis, what do you say to the objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, it was not limited to the Joint Command, and I'm thinking of General Vasiljevic's testimony about when he was sitting outside with General Ojdanic waiting to see Mr. Milosevic on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that testimony wasn't that he was going there to get instructions of any kind; he just saw him come out of a meeting with Milosevic. There's testimony that they were -- that they had some kinship relationship. We don't know what that meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we are satisfied that there is evidence from which the inference could be drawn that there was a failure to observe the strict command structure and that there is foundation for the question, and therefore we repel the objection. It might be best if you put the question again, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand - and I believe I understand the question - my answer is this: I am not aware of the fact that General Pavkovic ever went to see Milosevic. I simply don't know about that, and I can't base my conclusion on that, whether he complied with it or not. I'm talking based on my own personal experience. This is my personal view. Other than that, it is not my place to assess a corps commander in those terms. I know from personal experience, and I told you what it was like as far as I was concerned, in certain situations where because of haste I simply skipped his level of authority in that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It is late in the day, that's true, but I will further strain the Chamber's patience simply because there is a map that I must show the witness. Can we please have 4D381 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wish to supplement what I said earlier on. This is a map that I meant to show the witness during my chief, but it's only now that we have actually found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I recollect the difficulty. Thank you. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this what you initially referred to as 4D496 and said you would clarify the position and come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't think this map was on the original notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that may be the problem, Mr. Hannis, and therefore I understand your difficulty as well, but if Defence counsel were confused about the number then it's going to be omitted from the notification. We have to find a way of accommodating everyone's interests, and if it does raise a problem then, untidy though it may be, you will have another opportunity to cross-examine. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing before I broach that. This same map without the signature is P1578, it's an OTP exhibit. It was included in the notification. It is precisely because of this -- well, actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you tell us what you see on this map?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I see that this is about the decision to engage the forces of the Pristina Corps, to get them involved in Kosovo and Metohija. The decision was approved by the 3rd Army commander, General Samardzic. Probably we have the Pristina Corps commander's signature down there in the lower corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to pull it up a little bit for me to see the disposition and if all the formal aspects are met, because we did have a situation a while ago where the formal requirements were not met. Yes, this is precisely what we said a while ago in relation to that previous map because it was missing. This map was signed by the Pristina Corps commander, General Pavkovic. Given the fact that there was a need to depict the border belt and so on and so forth, there is a key for this map for it to be clearer. This is the disposition of the Pristina Corps forces following the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, I believe. After certain units were pulled out of Kosovo and Metohija, certain establishment units, the agreement was for three combat groups to remain in Dulje, Olujak [phoen], and Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything arising?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just a question: Is there a date on this map, General, indicating when it refers to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see it up there -- well, it's not really necessary for there to be the exact date and time on maps such as these because it has nothing to do with this position shown here. I didn't actually notice when it should actually be there, but it's not decisive. It's not about the day or the time of day. This is a fixed, permanent disposition. It stays like that for quite some time, especially in the border belt. It's possible. The instructions do say that we need a date there, but it's not really material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, is there a month or a year?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see it. If we pull it up, perhaps I could see, but right now I can't. I didn't notice the first time around. No, no date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this then, Mr. Mladenovic, a different form of map from the one we looked at earlier which had the name of the proposer omitted completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means. This is an excellent observation. In purely formal terms, this is done properly. The relevant commander signed this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it's done properly, but is it not a map of a completely different nature from the one that had not been done properly? Or are they similar maps are you saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess my question, Your Honour, would be: This appears to be a map showing deployments as opposed to a map depicting an operation or an action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a better way of putting the question. Are we not talking about in this case a map that simply sets out the disposition of forces, and in the other case with the proposer omitted a map which proposed an action for approval by the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the essential distinction. This is a disposition, it's stable, and the other map shows how a combat action is conducted or carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, anything further arising from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No more maps for this evening, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, am I right in understanding that you have only one more witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed you are, Your Honour, you're quite right. We believed -- we believe that we only have General Ljubisa Stojimirovic left. We were thinking about Dr. Petkovic, too, but we might start Stojimirovic tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if we do, have we time to deal with both of them should you decide to call both of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just one witness left. We're certain about that. We made efforts for the doctor to be here. Maybe I wasn't quite accurate in the way I put it. I apologise in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Bakrac, do you wish to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think it's quite self-evident and I don't want to come across as criticising my colleagues, but over the last several days the situation has taken a dramatic turn. The previous Defence team, wrapping up tomorrow as we see in their 65 ter notice, had a total of 72 hours for their examination-in-chief. In the notice that we received, there were a total of 14 witnesses, including the accused, General Pavkovic. For this week we have a list containing seven witnesses. By last night or by today, today is the first working day, we didn't even know that these seven witnesses would not be appearing next week, including General Pavkovic. Last Monday we sent word to both the parties and the Chamber that our client, General Lazarevic, after certain consultations decided to be the first witness to appear in his case, decided to appear and decided to appear before any other witnesses. Bearing in mind the fact that the evidence he is about to give will not be short, I'm not saying that it will be particularly lengthy, I'm not trying to scare you, we weren't really planning for any other witnesses to appear. Also since the VWS unit told us and instructed us that we shouldn't keep witnesses sitting here for more than seven days -- it's ten to 7.00 now. The gist of what I'm trying to say is this. We have a sudden change in the situation, and I must frankly tell the Chamber that we are not ready to get going with our evidence this coming Monday. Some of the things that we believed would be covered, and also bearing in mind the 65 ter notice, I must consider this together with my client, and there is also a technical problem that we discussed today. After consultations, we bridged our priority exhibit list, exhibits to be tendered through the accused himself. These will not be ready either because we have a deadline with the CLSS and we were supposed to start Monday, the 6th of November, which is the first Monday in the month of November. I'm not sure if I have provided sufficient reasons for you to understand the situation or if I should go on. I would appreciate any guidance from the Chamber. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't told us what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the notice that was served on Monday clearly stated that. I would like to ask the Chamber this, it's not just about what I desire, it's about you being prepared to grant this request. I would like General Lazarevic's defence to start according to plan, no matter how informal, to our original plan, which is Sunday, the 5th of November, or rather, Monday, the 6th of November -- or Tuesday, rather. I think the first day of the week is the 5th, but we don't sit on Monday, therefore that Tuesday. Your Honours, also, could I have just another two minutes. Today, to my fortune or misfortune, but I think fortune, we got the calculation of our time so far, the final date being the 13th of September, but I took into account the time we spent today. We have not crossed the 100-hour limit. And what I have in mind here is the pre-Defence Conference. I believe Your Honour said that we could divide this up among the Defence teams. Therefore, we have more than half the time left for a mere two Defence teams, and if we start the way I have just proposed, we're still ahead of the schedule, we are not behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I speak for myself when I make this comment just to ensure that you know what you have to address. The one thing that you've said that has any residence with me is that the change in circumstances requires you to consult with your client about the way in which his defence is presented. But that's not something that will take a particularly long time, bearing in mind the gaps we've had in this case to enable preparations to be made. So I don't at the moment see any reason why your case ought not to -- if you're making an opening, for example, and there's time tomorrow, I see no reason why your opening statement should not be tomorrow. If you need a day to consult with your client because you want to consider the approach, then that's different. It may be that you would then have the rest of tomorrow and perhaps Monday to deal with that because of the change in circumstances. But if you're looking for more -- and, of course, you're not going to require any witnesses until a week on Tuesday at least, by which time arrangements can be made to have your other witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid you did not understand me correctly, and I'm sure that only I am to blame because I failed to explain properly. It's not about consulting, it's not about the approach only, it's about the enormous number of topics that I have to go through with my client. We were supposed to have sufficient time to pursue that throughout the whole of the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This case has been running for 18 months more or less. You must be constantly updating your preparations to give evidence -- for your client to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you know, we had the military defences before we came along, and that brought about this change in circumstances, which affected our decision to have the accused appear first. And this very much hinged on the other Defences, too. Another result is that we are now cutting down our witness list. It wasn't certain at that time whether the accused would testify to begin with or whether he would be the first to appear. We covered part of the material, but we believed that other Defences would be covering some of the other material, and that is something that we have perhaps failed to cover. This is an enormous problem. We did have a meeting today and we won't have those documents before the week that I specified. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, we can cope with the documents, as you know, and have done so with others as the case has progressed knowing that the translations will be available. And so far as the time is concerned, your notice that you intimated on Monday says clearly that you still need the 122 hours you originally estimated. It says in terms that there's no alteration to the timing of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think that we understood each other well. There will be a change to the amount of time that we need. That is merely an estimate, 120 hours, but we've cut back on that. We certainly will be sticking to that sort of estimate, and one thing I can say that even with the deadline extension that we are now applying for, we shall be ready. I can't say 100 per cent certain, but I am quite certain that we shall be prepared to complete our case by the December break. And if we add that up, that doesn't add up to that sort of amount of hours. And we shall also be carving up our own time with the time allocated to the last Defence team. Even if we exceed that deadline, maybe next week we can deduce the -- we can deduct the ten-hour limit for the examination so that we might be ready to finally start our case. As for the opening statement, I did announce during the pre-Defence Conference that our opening statement would not take more than five or ten minutes, it will be a brief one. We did not wish to repeat any of the arguments put forward in the 98 bis. We shall be providing a very general idea about the course of our Defence case; therefore, it will not really take up that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're willing to hear from me briefly I have some sympathy for Mr. Bakrac because less than two weeks ago we had reason to think that there were going to be two other witnesses who well would have taken up probably five days at least between the two of them in cross-examination. In addition, those two witnesses probably were going to address a number of exhibits that Mr. Bakrac now has to consult with his client and decide whether they need to address those. At the same time I understand the Court's concern about losing a whole week, and I share that. I might propose an alternative that, originally, there were three other witnesses that were scheduled to testify and General Lazarevic was going to be fourth, those appear to be smaller or less-complicated witnesses, maybe there's a chance they could be brought here Wednesday or Thursday next week and we could do two or three witnesses toward the end of the week. General Lazarevic could testify, then, on Tuesday, the 6th, and I think his evidence would then still get nearly or identically the same weight you would give him for testifying first as opposed to testifying fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I clutch at this straw because I don't know if I'm reading your faces right and whether I can read what it is that you've decided. And now I'm not in an easy position because I was ready to criticise my colleague Mr. Hannis and now I see him jumping up to help me. Now I'm going to say what I had to say: Could we please be treated the same way the Prosecution was. I hope Mr. Hannis will not hold this against me, I am not criticising, I understand that, but on the week of the 12th of February, this week, they simply said, We don't have any witnesses this week, take our time, and we will continue next week. I believe that in the interests of justice we could allow for that possibility, and when we have this kind of argumentation it's not technical reasons. It was a difficult decision to have the accused person testify first, following the instructions of this Chamber that it would be useful for the Chamber. Now after all and after my promise that this would not in any way interfere with our deadline, I wouldn't really want to lose this very last straw that I've been clutching at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll appreciate that we've always been concerned that having time in the bank is a great benefit for later in the case, and the circumstances you've just identified were the type of circumstances we would envisage arising in the Defence case as well. Mr. Hannis got a hard time from the Bench earlier in the case, and it was only latterly in desperate straits that he got some sympathy. So you may not necessarily wish to be treated the same way as he was in truth. We might be assisted a little if we knew what the timing of the sixth accused case was likely to be, but if you sit down we may hear something from Mr. Lukic, who's meanwhile hiding behind you. Can you help at all, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm not ready to take any heat at this moment. I would rather have it dumped on Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, if he were to finish by the recess and you were to take up the sort of hinted three months or so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In three months we would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- using more time than any other accused. And you may feel that you can reassure us that your evidence is not likely to exceed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't like to make promises if I'm not hundred per cent sure that I can keep them, but as you know we'll do our best to concentrate our evidence. I know that it might not be good enough if it's our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you -- well, that's being unfair to yourselves. But you know that it's not been our practice to compel parties to behave in a particular way, but we have encouraged all of you to give careful consideration to what you're doing and always to bear time in mind.
